analysis.title: Big win for Democrats
key_insights: Democrats are poised to win majorities in both the House and Senate in the 3 November 2026 midterms, a larger shift than most polls projected. Commerzbank says the margin is decisive enough to end debate over election manipulation, and Trump has acknowledged the defeat.
House count per AP as of 07:00 CET: Democrats 209 seats, Republicans 124, 102 races undecided. Republicans previously held a 219-214 majority with two vacancies.

Senate: Republicans held 53-47 before the election (independents counted with Democrats). Democrats have gained at least six seats, in Ohio, South Carolina, North Carolina, Kansas, Iowa and Texas. The Texas Democratic candidate leads by 12 points, and Maine is a possible further gain.
Commerzbank attributes the result mainly to high inflation, which polls named as the main negative issue, plus Trump's low popularity. Solid growth and a stable labor market took a back seat.
Republican governors were voted out in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, states that are promoting data center expansion. Commerzbank says this could slow data center expansion plans.

Democrats have little room to legislate. Many Senate decisions need 60 votes, and a presidential veto could only be overridden by two-thirds of both chambers. Commerzbank expects a far-reaching legislative blockade, including for Republican plans on deregulation, tax cuts and social benefit reforms.

A Democratic Senate can block Trump appointments, including Federal Reserve governors. Powell must vacate his governor seat by January 2028 at the latest, and Commerzbank says a Democratic Senate would prevent a Trump loyalist taking it. It calls this a decisive setback for Trump's attack on Fed independence.

With Congress closed to him, Trump is expected to rely on executive orders and foreign policy. Commerzbank expects tariffs to stay, with other legal bases sought after court defeats, and says more active foreign policy could be unpleasant for Europe.

Budget conflict risk remains high, possibly triggered by financing of the Iran war. Federal funding runs on transitional financing until 11 December 2026, after which a regular budget or another continuing resolution is needed, or a shutdown follows, as in Q4 2025.

Democratic majorities enable committee chairs and investigations of the Trump administration. Commerzbank says the outcome of those investigations is open and the Department of Justice could let some fizzle out.

Intra-party debate among Democrats continues. The DSA-aligned left wing may feel vindicated, while moderates won in typically Republican areas. A California billionaire wealth tax proposal was probably rejected, with 57% against after half the votes were counted.
risk_factors: Government shutdown risk if no budget or continuing resolution is passed before the 11 December 2026 funding deadline.
Budget conflicts, possibly over financing of the Iran war.
Legislative gridlock between a Democratic Congress and Trump's veto.
Slower data center expansion in states that voted out Republican governors.
Tariff policy continues through executive action.

geopolitical: Trump is expected to focus more on foreign policy and executive orders after the midterm loss, which Commerzbank says could become unpleasant for Europe given policy differences with most European governments.

tension_points.bull_case: Democrats gain committee chairs, investigation powers and can block Trump appointments, including Fed governors, which Commerzbank calls a decisive setback for Trump's attack on Fed independence.
tension_points.bear_case: The 60-vote Senate threshold and presidential veto power leave Democrats little room to pass legislation, so Commerzbank expects a far-reaching legislative blockade.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Congress could only override a veto with two-thirds majorities in both chambers, which Commerzbank calls unrealistic.

theme_stances.evidence: A Democratic majority in the Senate would certainly prevent a Trump loyalist
